newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapatista says Chiapas peace depends on Indian rights.
newsitem.headline: Zapatista says Chiapas peace depends on Indian rights.

text.p: Zapatista rebel leader Subcommander Marcos has called a Mexican government proposal on Indian rights a "cruel and insolent hoax" that threatens to undermine peace talks in the southern state of Chiapas.

The government has proposed constitutional changes to protect Indian rights based on a previous agreement with the Zapatistas, a predominantly Maya Indian rebel force that rose up in arms in January, 1994.

But the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN) rejected the government's proposal as "inacceptable," saying it violates the letter and spirit of those accords, which were reached last year after months of arduous negotiations.
Further peace talks to end the conflict were suspended four months ago with little sign of agreement.
For the time being, the Zapatistas appear content to retreat to their jungle stronghold, where they are surrounded by the Mexican army as a ceasefire holds.

"It's a cruel and insolent hoax for the struggle of the Indian people of Mexico, a mockery of the will for dialogue of the EZLN and the effort of Cocopa (the government negotiating commission)," Marcos told a news conference late on Saturday.
As is his trademark style, Marcos arrived at the news conference on horseback wearing a ski mask and smoking a pipe.

"The government counterproposal puts the entire peace process in Mexico in crisis," said Marcos, who is not an Indian but has become internationally known as the radical chic symbol of the Zapatista cause..
The government of President Ernesto Zedillo immediately rejected the rebel position, saying in a statement that it has conducted itself with "utmost seriousness and responsibility."

It said the proposed constitutional reforms, written to match its agreement with the Zapatistas, grant automony to Indian communities, preserve their customs, allow them to chose their own leaders and grant them special access to natural resources.
The Zapatistas considered the proposals "racist, ethnocentric and discriminatory" and said they were happier with the text of an agreement signed with the Cocopa commission nearly a year ago.
The government said that text was modified to accommodate legal technicalities, but added that it would make new efforts to have "a dignified peace and justice prevail in Chiapas."
One member of Cocopa, opposition Congressman Rodolfo Elizondo, told reporters in Chiapas the commission has asked the Zapatistas to take more time to consider the government proposal.
The Zapatista guerrillas had been training in the Chiapas jungle for years before launching their uprising on Jan. 1, 1994 and seizing several of the largest towns in Chiapas.
After 11 days of combat that killed an estimated 145 people, the government declared a unilateral ceasefire. The two sides finally sat down together in April 1995 to start peace talks.
